newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS-NO SPEEDY END TO S.AFRICAN FOREX CONTROLS - STALS.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-NO SPEEDY END TO S.AFRICAN FOREX CONTROLS - STALS.

text.p: South African Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals on Friday threw cold water on hopes for an early lifting of foreign exchange controls, saying the process was likely to take between four and five years.
He also ruled out a "big bang" or one-off scrapping of rand controls.
Ending capital restrictions was linked to implementation of of the government's macro-economic strategy, known as GEAR (Growth, Employment and Redistribution), itself a gradual process.
"These things will be done over the next four to five years. Therefore exchange controls will be dismantled over the next four to five years," he told Reuters in an interview.

"It's part of the programme. If we we have big inflows of capital next year we can go a lot faster, but that applies to all the other things in that programme. Exchange control abolition is part of the the consistent programme of GEAR and GEAR is a four- to five-year programme."

Commenting on an interview he gave to Business Day newspaper earlier this week, where he talked about conditions for a "big bang" scrapping of controls, Stals said his aim had been to explain why this option was not feasible.
"I was trying to explain why we cannot have a big bang...The only way to do it is to do it gradually," he said while attending a conference.
Dealers had been wrong in trying to detect a split between him and Finance Minister Trevor Manuel.
Stals said he agreed with Manuel that some "prudential" requirements might still be needed restricting the movement of cash offshore by funds, to ensure they had adequate local cover for liabilities.
Low reserves continued to hamper moves to ease exchange controls and Stals said he would ideally like three months' import cover in place -- equivalent to 30 billion rand.
"But that certainly is not the policy. The policy is a little bit of this and a little bit of that," he added.
Sputh African markets took some heart on Friday from news that October's official reserves rose marginally to 10.28 billion rand from 10.04 billion in September.
But analysts said the figures had been inflated from proceeds of government issues and reserves only represented a meagre four weeks' import cover.
Low reserves have been a target for speculators selling the rand in the belief that the authorities lack the ammunition to defend the currency.
The latest selling wave took the unit to an all-time low of 4.77 against the dollar last week -- a drop of over 30 percent since mid-February -- although it has since recovered to around 4.70.
Stals said the sharp fall in the rand raised the risk of inflation and said fighting price rises had to be the prime goal of South African monetary policy.
As a result, interest rates would have to stay high.
"More so than at any other time in the past eight years, the monetary authorities will now have to use all the powers at their disposal to fight inflation in South Africa," he told the conference.

South Africa's key Bank rate cxurrently stands at 16 percent. Until last month, there had been hopes of a rate cut. But the latest fall in the rand and a money market squeeze raised fears that the next move will in fact be up.
